                    Regime

                    Where we are

                    Ray Dalio's four economic environments, mapped to today. Growth is still holding up and inflation is rising with oil. That corner rewards commodities and inflation-linked assets and punishes nominal bonds and long-duration growth stocks.

                    Inflation rising ↑
                    Growth ↓ · Inflation ↑

                    Stagflation

                    Works: inflation-linked bonds, commodities, gold, cash. Hurts: equities and nominal bonds together.

                    Growth ↑ · Inflation ↑

                    Inflationary boom

                    Works: commodities, energy, value equities, inflation-linked bonds. Hurts: nominal bonds, long-duration growth.

                    We are here, edging left
                    Growth ↓ · Inflation ↓

                    Deflationary bust

                    Works: nominal bonds, cash, quality equities. Hurts: credit, commodities, cyclicals.

                    Growth ↑ · Inflation ↓

                    Goldilocks

                    Works: equities, corporate credit, nominal bonds. Hurts: commodities and gold, relatively.

                    Sources

                    Where the scraper looks

                    Edit feeds.toml to add a Substack, a Telegram channel, an X account or any RSS feed. Telegram is read from each public channel's web preview; X only through its official API, with the X_BEARER_TOKEN secret. Each source carries a tier: official, niche, specialist or mainstream.

                    How a theme is scoredHeat = (n24h − mean28d) ÷ max(sd28d, √(mean28d + 1)): the Poisson floor stops one mention on a quiet theme from looking hot. Niche skew = share of the last 72 hours' mentions from niche and specialist sources − that tier's share of everything read. Lead = the lag, 0 to 5 days, at which niche mentions best predict mainstream mentions (cross-correlation above 0.3, with 21 days of history). Novelty = share of today's distinctive words the theme has not used before. Noteworthy = heat ≥ 2, or skew above 20 points across two or more platforms.

                    Plumbing

                    Liquidity and funding

                    Net liquidity is the Fed's balance sheet minus the Treasury's cash account and the overnight reverse repo facility: roughly the cash the Fed leaves in the private system. SOFR against the rate the Fed pays on reserves (IORB) says whether that cash is getting scarce. The Fed stopped shrinking its balance sheet on Dec 1, 2025, citing money-market conditions. Federal Reserve

                    Net liquidity is an accounting identity, not a law of stock prices. Use it for the plumbing (who is draining cash, and how close reserves are to scarce), not to time the index.

                    Price of protection

                    Is insurance cheap?

                    Implied volatility is what an option charges; realized volatility is what the market delivered. The gap is the volatility risk premium: on average buyers of protection pay sellers for carrying crash risk. The desk buys convexity when it is cheap, not when it is needed.

                    Desk rules: buy convexity when implied sits in the bottom third of its ten-year range and within about two points of its median premium; prefer put spreads and collars when implied is in the top fifth; when the VIX curve inverts, stress is priced now, so monetize in stages instead of buying.

                    Tool

                    Tail-hedge budget

                    Taleb's trade in one table: a small, steady premium that buys a large payout in a crash. Roll out-of-the-money puts on the full book and see what a year of insurance costs against what one bad quarter pays.

                    Out-of-the-money puts usually trade at a higher implied volatility than at-the-money options; the default allows for that skew.

                    Risk mitigation

                    Match the hedge to the disease.

                    Long bonds cure a growth scare and worsen an inflation shock. Puts pay in any crash and bleed in calm markets. Trend-following earns its keep in slow, persistent moves. The matrix grades fifteen hedges against six scenarios; select any cell for the reasoning.

                    Mechanism

                    Two kinds of AI selloff

                    Whether long Treasuries help depends on why the book is falling. Long yields react to the cause of the selloff, and the two causes push them in opposite directions.

                    Growth scare

                    Bonds hedge
                    1. AI revenue or demand disappoints
                    2. Growth and rate expectations fall
                    3. Long yields drop
                    4. TLT rallies while the book falls

                    Oct 8, 2026. Reports of weak OpenAI revenue hit AI names; the Nasdaq-100 fell 1.39%. The 30-year yield fell 5.9bp, worth about +0.9% on a bond with TLT's 15.5-year duration.

                    investingLive

                    Financing or inflation shock

                    Bonds fail
                    1. Oil, capex debt or fiscal supply push inflation and issuance up
                    2. Term premium rises; the Fed hikes
                    3. Long yields climb
                    4. TLT falls with the book

                    March 2026. As the Iran war closed the Strait of Hormuz, the S&P 500 fell 5.1% and a 10-year Treasury position lost about 2.0% in the same month. Dec 12, 2025. The Nasdaq-100 fell 1.9% on AI capex worries while the 10-year yield rose 4bp.

                    Federal Reserve · Plastics Industry Association · Bloomberg via Swissinfo

                    A hedge removes at most ρ² of the book's variance: 9% at a −0.3 correlation. Long bonds protect against a scenario; options and lower gross protect against the drawdown itself.

                    Rules

                    Survival rules the engine enforces

                    1. Ruin is the only unrecoverable loss.Size so the 95th-percentile one-year drawdown stays inside the limit, before any view on return. (Taleb's ergodicity point: a bet you cannot repeat forever is not worth its average.)
                    2. Barbell the book.Very safe on one side (bills, TIPS), very convex on the other (options, the concentrated AI sleeve). Avoid the fragile middle: leveraged carry that loses everything in one gap.
                    3. Prefer contracts to correlations.A put pays by contract. A bond hedge pays only if the correlation holds, and it flipped in 2022 and again in 2026.
                    4. Trim on rules.A position that runs 20% over its target weight gets cut back to target. Sell in pieces; never all or nothing.
                    5. Know the rate exposure every day.Every name carries a rates beta; the book's total is reported daily next to the hedge ratio.

                    Field guide

                    Every security is a bundle of a few risks.

                    Rates, credit, equity, inflation, volatility, liquidity and currency. Know which ones a security carries, where it sits in the capital structure, and what job it does in the book before you size it.

                    Capital structure

                    Who gets paid first

                    Paid first · lower yield
                    Senior secured loansFloatingFirst claim on collateral. Leveraged loans and most private credit live here.
                    Senior unsecured bondsIG and high yieldThe bulk of corporate debt, including the hyperscalers' bond deals.
                    Subordinated debtJunior notesPaid after senior creditors; bank capital notes sit here.
                    Convertible bondsDebt plus a callA bond with an equity option attached; lower coupon in exchange for upside.
                    Preferred stockFixed or floating dividendStrategy's STRC pays a 12.00% variable dividend semi-monthly, reset to keep it near $100 par.
                    Common equityResidual claimEverything left after every claim above is paid.
                    Options and warrantsDerivativesClaims on the equity itself: the most convex, the most likely to expire worthless.
                    Paid last · higher expected return
                    STRC rate: Strategy Inc 8-K, Aug 31, 2026
                    The seven risk drivers
                    Rates
                    Price falls when yields rise. Measured by duration and DV01.
                    Credit
                    Loss if the issuer defaults or its spread widens.
                    Equity
                    Exposure to the residual value of a business.
                    Inflation
                    Real value lost, or protected, as prices rise.
                    Volatility
                    Value that moves with the size of price swings rather than their direction.
                    Liquidity
                    Cost and delay of selling when you need to.
                    Currency
                    Value changes from the exchange rate alone.

                    Insurers & balance sheets

                    The market's long-duration buyers are becoming the AI buildout's lenders.

                    Insurers collect premiums today and pay claims years later. That float makes them natural buyers of long-dated debt and, increasingly, of private credit and data-center bonds. Watch them for two signals: where long-end demand comes from, and where credit risk is quietly piling up.

                    Model

                    How an insurer makes money

                    Collect

                    Float

                    Premiums arrive before claims are paid. Berkshire's float was about $177.5B at June 30, 2026, money it invests but does not own.

                    Match

                    Duration

                    Life and annuity liabilities run decades, so insurers buy long bonds and private loans to match them. That makes them price-setters for the long end.

                    Earn

                    Two engines

                    Profit = underwriting result + investment spread. Higher yields raise the second engine; credit losses hit it.

                    Trading · prop

                    Edge is a number. Measure it before you size it.

                    Prop trading is three numbers: how much each trade earns after costs, how many trades it takes to prove that, and how much to risk so a bad run cannot end the game. The tools below compute all three, simulate a funded-account challenge, and follow a pod shop's gross return down to what its investors keep.

                    Industry

                    Who earns what

                    The largest liquidity providers are posting records, while most retail challenge-takers never see a payout.

                    Virtu, Q2 2026 adjusted net trading income$717.9M+26% on a year; market making $579.9M. About $11.6M a trading day over 62 sessions (computed).Virtu 8-K, Q2 2026

                    Tool

                    Edge calculator

                    Win rate and payoff in R, where 1 R is the amount risked on a trade. Costs come off every trade. The chart is long-run growth by risk per trade: it rises to the Kelly fraction, then falls, and past twice Kelly it loses money even with an edge.

                    Expectancy
                    Break-even win rate
                    Sharpe, a year
                    Time to prove it (t = 2)

                    Edge arithmeticE = pb − (1 − p) − c R a trade. Break-even p = (1 + c) ÷ (1 + b). Trades to prove it: n = (2·sd ÷ E)2. Kelly f* = p − (1 − p) ÷ b. Growth a trade at risk r: g = p ln(1 + r(b − c)) + (1 − p) ln(1 − r(1 + c)).

                    Tool

                    Prop challenge simulator

                    A funded-account evaluation is a race between a profit target and two loss limits. Three thousand simulated attempts show the pass rate at your risk, and the risk that maximizes it.

                    Process

                    The trader's day

                    1. Before the open: write the limits down.Daily loss limit, size per trade, the three names you will trade. A limit set mid-loss is not a limit.
                    2. Every trade gets a reason and an exit.Log the hypothesis and the price that proves it wrong in the decision journal before entry.
                    3. Size from the edge, then shrink.Quarter Kelly at most, and never more than the challenge-optimal risk while proving the edge.
                    4. Stop at the daily limit.The simulator shows most failures are a breach, not a missed target.
                    5. Score process, not P&L.Brier, hit rate and payoff over 30 trades; the journal's luck test says when a streak means anything.

                    Trading · market making

                    Market makers sell immediacy and refuse to warehouse risk.

                    The spread pays for three things: being picked off by better-informed traders, holding inventory while prices move, and running the machine. The best market makers win on the first two. The tools below quote like Avellaneda and Stoikov, price adverse selection like Glosten and Milgrom, and execute like Almgren and Chriss.

                    Tool

                    Quote like Avellaneda and Stoikov

                    Six hundred simulated trading days. The inventory-skewed quoter shades its prices against what it already holds; the symmetric one quotes the same spread around the mid. Same expected spread, very different risk.

                    Mean P&L, skewed vs symmetric
                    P&L spread
                    Mean ÷ spread
                    Inventory swings

                    Avellaneda and Stoikov (2008)Reservation price r = s − qγσ2(T − t). Total spread δ = γσ2(T − t) + (2/γ) ln(1 + γ/k). Fills arrive at rate Ae−kδ at distance δ from the mid.

                    Tool

                    Adverse selection: who is on the other side

                    Glosten and Milgrom: if a share μ of orders comes from traders who know where the price is going, the spread must cover what they take. Retail flow is mostly uninformed, which is why it is worth paying for.

                    Break-even spread
                    Edge per trade

                    Glosten and Milgrom (1985), two valuesBreak-even spread = μ(Vhigh − Vlow). Edge per trade = spread/2 − μ(Vhigh − Vlow)/2.

                    Tool

                    Execution: the square-root law and the optimal schedule

                    Impact grows with the square root of size: four times the order costs twice the impact per share. Trading slowly saves impact and buys timing risk; the Almgren-Chriss schedule finds the best trade-off for your urgency.

                    Square-root impact
                    With half the spread
                    Your schedule: cost ± risk

                    Impact and scheduleImpact = Yσdaily√(Q/ADV), Y of order 1 (Tóth et al., 2011). Almgren-Chriss holdings xj = X sinh(κ(T − tj)) / sinh(κT), cosh(κτ) = 1 + λσ2τ2/(2η). Linear temporary impact η is calibrated so the even pace costs exactly the square-root impact.

                    Reading the tape

                    The book's own liquidity

                    Three estimators from daily bars: Roll's effective spread from the bounce in closing prices, Amihud's price move per dollar traded, and Kyle's lambda, the slope of price on signed volume.

                    EstimatorsRoll spread = 2√(−cov(Δpt, Δpt−1)) when the covariance is negative. Amihud = mean(|r| ÷ dollar volume) per $1M. Kyle λ = cov(r, signed $ volume) ÷ var(signed $ volume), sign from the tick rule.

                    Tool · execution lab

                    Fill quality: was that passive fill any good?

                    A fill at the bid looks like a win until the midpoint moves. The markout splits the result into the edge at the fill and the move after it, and the posting decision weighs the chance of filling against the cost of missing. Illustrative book: $100.00 bid for 900 shares, $100.02 offered for 100.

                    Markout of the passive buy
                    Midpoint
                    Queue imbalance
                    Size-weighted midpoint

                    Markout and the posting decisionm = (a + b)/2, I = (Qb − Qa)/(Qb + Qa), m̃ = (aQb + bQa)/(Qb + Qa). Mh = s(mt − pt) + s(mt+h − mt). Vpost = P(F)(E[Mh | F] − cF) − (1 − P(F))Cmiss.

                    Eight working theses, each with a way to be wrong.

                    A thesis earns capital only with evidence, an expression, a hedge, and data that would change the desk's mind. These are research positions for the engine to test, not recommendations.

                    Lenses

                    Borrowed minds, turned into rules.

                    The desk reads widely and keeps only what it can encode. Each lens below is paraphrased in one line, then mapped to the rule or view where the engine uses it.

                    The thinkers

                    Desk principles

                    From a market maker's advice

                    Notes from a conversation with a trader who built his own prop firm and market-making business.

                    1. Process over P&L.Nobody cares that you were up 15% last year. They want to see the system they could plug into theirs.
                    2. Data first, then judgment.Build the tool, use it, then ask whether the answer makes sense.
                    3. Trim, don't dump.Break positions into pieces; a winner can be cut 20% without an all-or-nothing call.
                    4. Always know your rate exposure.Watch long bonds against growth stocks; the relationship decides whether your hedge exists.
                    5. Speed of learning is the edge.Pattern recognition and a fast observe-decide-act loop beat any single model.
                    6. Choose who you go to battle with.Proximity to sharp people compounds faster than any position.

                    The board

                    Today's decisions

                    Seven calls the desk makes every morning. Live inputs replace the dated snapshot after each daily run.

                    ConfidenceConfidence in a call = ∏ pi over the assumptions it rests on (independence makes this a floor when the assumptions move together). Flip distance = |threshold − level|; weeks to flip = distance ÷ velocity when the velocity points at the threshold.

                    Rates of change

                    How fast each signal is moving, and when its rule fires

                    Level says where a market is. Velocity says where it is going, acceleration says whether it is speeding up, and time to trigger says when the rule fires if the pace holds. A 13-week pace that disagrees with the 4-week pace is a turn in progress.

                    Velocity, acceleration, time to triggerv13 = least-squares slope of the last 13 weeks of prints, per week. a = v13(now) − v13(13 weeks ago). T = (L* − L) ÷ v weeks, defined only when v points at the line L*. A least-squares slope uses every print in the window, so one bad print moves it far less than a two-point change.

                    Weighted assumptions

                    What has to be true, how likely it is, and what breaks if it is not

                    Fragility = (1 − p) × impact. The most fragile assumptions sit at the top. Move a slider to change your own probability; every decision that rests on it updates.

                    Probabilities are the desk's judgment, written down so they can be argued with. Each row names the evidence and the test that would falsify it. Your changes stay in this browser.

                    Known knowns to unknown unknowns

                    What we know, what we know we don't, and what we pretend not to

                    Each quadrant gets a different response. Facts get acted on, ranges get sized, blind spots get audited, and the unknowable gets prepared for, never predicted.

                    Second to fourth order

                    Five shocks, run to the fourth order

                    Keynes's beauty contest, applied: the first order is what everyone sees; the money is in what the first order forces others to do. Each step names what to watch, with today's reading, and what to do at that order.

                    Rules and probabilities are the desk's judgment, stated so they can be argued with. Research desk, not investment advice.

                    Decide · the solver

                    From evidence to a sized choice, with every step shown.

                    Seven observed signals update the odds of seven three-month scenarios. A search over 18,414 portfolios finds the one with the highest expected log growth that keeps the worst scenario inside your loss limit. Then the desk plays the same choice against an adversarial Nature, prices what each signal is worth to learn, and finds the most plausible way to breach the limit.

                      Robust to being wrong about the odds

                      What the solver chooses if its own probabilities might be off

                      Solving under doubt…

                      The choice at each level of doubt

                      Doubt is a Kullback-Leibler radius around the posterior odds: the solver maximizes the worst expected log growth over every set of odds that close. Guaranteed growth is that worst case; the price is the nominal growth given up to get it.

                      Reverse stress

                      The most plausible way to breach the limit

                      Ordinary stress tests ask what a given shock does. This asks which joint move of stocks, the AI factor, yields, oil and gold produces the loss with the smallest Mahalanobis distance, using covariances measured in each inflation regime.

                      Estimated
                      FactorMove

                      Closest breachs* = −L Σb ÷ (b′Σb), distance d = L ÷ √(b′Σb), where b is the book's first-order exposure to each factor. First order only: the put spread and the bond's convexity are not in b.

                      Scenarios, likelihoods and the AI factor's volatility are assumptions; covariances are measured. The solver is exact on its grid, not between grid points.

                      Decide · game theory

                      Other players choose too. Their best response moves your book.

                      The capex race is a prisoner's dilemma calibrated to the builders' filings. A crowded trade unwinds like a bank run with a computable threshold. A market maker prices your order as if you might know something. Each model has a closed form, solved here exactly.

                      Capex race

                      Why every builder overbuilds

                      Five builders choose capacity; the return on capacity falls as total capacity rises (Cournot). Each builder's cost of $1 of capacity a year is depreciation over its stated server life plus its cost of capital. The model is calibrated so its equilibrium reproduces the builders' actual trailing capex.

                      Hypothesis The return on capacity and the cost of capital are assumptions; capex is observed from filings.

                      Overbuild vs one coordinated buyer
                      Profit the five keep
                      A sixth builder cuts profit
                      Return: race vs coordinated

                      One seat at the table: profit a year

                      Cournot with N firmsP = a − bQ; qi = (a − (N+1)ci + Σcj) ÷ (b(N+1)); symmetric: industry profit is 4N ÷ (N+1)2 of the joint maximum (56% at N = 5) and capacity is 2N ÷ (N+1) times it (1.67x).

                      Crowded exit

                      When a crowded trade runs

                      Pods in the same trade each get a private read of its edge and a common public one. Staying pays the edge minus the fire-sale loss from everyone who leaves; leaving costs the exit. This is a global game (Morris and Shin): there is a threshold read below which a pod exits, and it is unique when private views are precise relative to public news.

                      Share of the crowd exiting
                      Fire-sale cost if all exit
                      Exit threshold
                      Equilibrium

                      Global gameθ ~ N(y, 1/α), xi = θ + ε, ε ~ N(0, 1/β). The marginal pod at x* is indifferent: E[θ | x*] − λΦ(√β(x* − μ*) ÷ √(1 + β/(α+β))) = −c, with λ = Yσ√(crowd ÷ volume). Diffuse public news gives the Laplace limit x* = λ/2 − c.

                      Market maker against an informed trader

                      What your order tells the market

                      In Kyle's model the market maker cannot tell informed from uninformed flow, so she moves the price in proportion to net orders. The informed trader trades just enough to stay hidden in the noise.

                      Price impact (Kyle's lambda)
                      Your order moves the price
                      Informed profit

                      Kyle (1985)λ = σv ÷ (2σu), β = σu ÷ σv, informed profit σuσv ÷ 2; prices end up revealing half of the private information.

                        The brain · higher-order thinking, computed

                        Carry every assumption to its fourth-order conclusion.

                              Frontier reasoning

                              Which world, how surprised, what if, and how it breaks

                              How surprised should the brain be?

                                The readings' distance from what the map expects (Mahalanobis, against a chi-square), and each reading's z-score when the others predict it (exact leave-one-out). A surprising day means a cause the map does not have.

                                But for each cause, where would the book be?

                                Each inferred cause's contribution to the book's implied move; removing it leaves the rest. In a linear map these are exact Shapley values and they add up to the whole.

                                Which channels carry it

                                  Had it been otherwise

                                  A counterfactual, not a forecast: it keeps everything today's evidence says about the other causes, changes one thing, and re-runs the world (Pearl's abduction, action, prediction).

                                    Learning from the data

                                    Does the data agree with the map's own assumptions?

                                    Learning from 440 months of data…

                                    The causal order, assumed against learned

                                    How often each pair keeps its order (200 resamples, 1990 to 2021)

                                    DirectLiNGAM: with non-Gaussian shocks, a cause is the variable whose regression residuals look independent of it, which no Gaussian method can tell. It assumes linear links and no hidden common cause, so read disagreements as questions, not verdicts.

                                    What each asset did in stocks' worst months, by regime

                                    Average 3-month-change z-score in the 10% of months when stocks fell most. A hedge earns its place by what it does here, not on average.

                                    Who predicts whom (Granger, 1990 to 2021)

                                      Two lags of one series improving the forecast of another, F-test at 5%. Predictive precedence, not proof of cause; read beside the learned order.

                                      How fragile is each measured link?

                                      Least squares against a Huber fit that lets big months count linearly, t-statistics with Newey-West errors that do not assume independent months, and the number of the most influential months that, dropped, would reverse the sign (each count checked by refitting; "over 10%" means it would not reverse). A link that flips on three months is a hypothesis, however large its t.

                                      Self-checks

                                      How far to trust the brain

                                      Do its 90% error bars hold? Every month predicted from earlier months only, 2000 on

                                      Textbook: the ensemble's Gaussian interval. Conformal: adaptive conformal inference (Gibbs and Candès, 2021), whose width is the 90% quantile of past standardized errors and whose target adapts after every miss, so coverage stays near 90% even when the world shifts. "Honest width now" is the conformal half-width over the textbook one.

                                      Which world model the data trusts, scored out of sample

                                      Five rival models of each measured equation: full-history least squares, the last 36 months only, an outlier-resistant Huber fit, links that drift (Kalman filter), and no link at all. Stacking (Yao, Vehtari, Simpson and Gelman, 2018) picks the mixture with the best out-of-sample log score; each month's weights use earlier months only.

                                      What would an unseen common cause have to explain to erase each link?

                                      The robustness value (Cinelli and Hazlett, 2020): the share of the residual variance of both the parent and the child that a confounder would have to explain to drive the link to zero, and in brackets to make it insignificant at 5%. Compare it with the strongest observed parent: a hidden cause stronger than anything measured is possible, but it is a claim to argue, not a default.

                                                      4 · Act

                                                      Proposals, what to watch, and when to look again

                                                      Proposals (for a person to review)
                                                        Watch, then loop

                                                          Positions · Fundamentals, accounting and what the price requires

                                                          Is the market being rational about each name, and if not, why?

                                                          For each holding: the accounting under the earnings, the growth today's price requires by reverse DCF, how often companies that size have ever done it, the case the price is right and the case it is wrong, each in points of required growth.

                                                          How it is computedEnterprise value = market value − cash + debt. Free cash flow margin moves in a straight line from today's (after stock pay) to the steady-state margin (what the business throws off when it stops growing: the lower of after-tax operating earnings and operating cash flow − D&A − stock pay, over revenue, so customer prepayments, deferred taxes and other timing do not flatter it) over ten years; terminal growth 3%; discount rate = 10-year yield + beta × 4.5% equity premium, blended with after-tax debt. The implied growth solves PV = EV by bisection. Base rates: Mauboussin, Callahan and Majd, The Base Rate Book (2016), 10-year real sales CAGR by starting size, 1950 to 2015; implied nominal growth less 2.5% inflation is compared with them.

                                                          Reported figures are trailing twelve months from each company's latest filing as collected; prices are a dated market snapshot. Assumptions are labelled. Research on a model book, not advice.

                                                            Scorecard

                                                            Luck or skill?

                                                            Closed decisions only. With fewer than 20, read every number as a hint, not a verdict.

                                                            Process against outcomeOutcome = return after the market's share (beta)

                                                            Good process means at least three of four: logged before entry, sized by the rule, kill line respected, two independent sources. Judge the process, not the outcome (Annie Duke calls the opposite "resulting").

                                                            The scorecardBrier = (1/n) ∑ (pi − yi)2: 0 is perfect, 0.25 is a coin flip. Alphai = ri − βi rbench; t = mean(alpha) ÷ (sd/√n). Luck test: P(at least k hits in n | coin flip). Decisions needed for t = 2: (2·sd ÷ mean)2. Kelly: f* = p − (1 − p) ÷ b, with b = win ÷ loss.

                                                            Your entries are private to you: in the published page they live in your own space on the artifact (no one else can read them, the owner included); elsewhere they stay in this browser. Examples are illustrative and never saved.

                                                            Swans · Fat tails and the hedges that survive them

                                                            You cannot predict the tail. You can own it cheaply.

                                                            A normal model says a six-sigma month comes once in 84 million years. Since 1871 the S&P 500 has had two. The desk's answer is Taleb's: name the gray swans you can, own convexity for the ones you can't, and never size so that one of them is ruin.

                                                            Lab

                                                            Does the hedge pay for itself? The compound-growth test

                                                            Mark Spitznagel's test: a tail hedge is worth owning only if the book's compound growth is higher with it than without it. A hedge can lose money on average and still raise compound growth, because it shrinks the losses that compounding punishes most.

                                                            Compound growthg = exp(∑ ps ln(1 + rs − c + hs)) − 1, where c is the hedge cost and hs its payoff in scenario s.

                                                            Swans are illustrative of exposures, not predictions. Hedge costs are typical ranges, not quotes.

                                                            Coverage, from the filings

                                                            Who funds the build from cash flow, and who does not

                                                            Descriptive coverage categories from one year of filings (the Minsky framing, without the verdict): cash flow against capex and interest. Capex above cash flow is a funding gap, not proof of distress; cash, asset sales, discretionary spending and debt maturities all matter, and maturities are not modelled here.

                                                            Earnings quality

                                                            Paper profits: earnings from marking each other up

                                                            Non-operating income is mostly gains on stakes in other AI companies. It counts in earnings per share, it is reflexive (it rises with the boom), and it reverses faster than the business.

                                                            The depreciation wave

                                                            What today's capex adds to tomorrow's costs

                                                            Capex hits the income statement later, as depreciation. The model below is fitted to each company's reported depreciation, then run forward on its guidance, at the stated server life and at a shorter one.

                                                            The modelEach year's capex Cv enters service mid-year; a share s depreciates over the server life Ls, the rest over 25 years. Dt = ∑v Cv [ s·overlap(t, v, Ls)/Ls + (1 − s)·overlap(t, v, 25)/25 ]. s is solved so the model reproduces the reported depreciation in the fit year. Land and construction in progress are not separated, so the wave arrives later than modeled.

                                                            Bottom line

                                                            What the engine changed because of the manual

                                                            1. A regime module with a gross scaler.Rule 7a.1 now reads policy direction and real yields; today it caps gross at 0.90x to 1.13x, looser than the volatility rule's 0.71x, so volatility binds.
                                                            2. A hedge selector by expected shortfall per dollar of carry.Since 1990, with inflation above the 2.75% line, the 10-year Treasury removed nothing from the worst-month loss; a put spread removed the most.
                                                            3. Student-t shortfall and five scenario replays.The normal model understates the worst 2.5% of months by about a third.
                                                            4. Red flags from the filings.Capex over depreciation, cash conversion, stock pay and receivables, for every builder, every day.
                                                            5. A physical-versus-futures oil check.The manual's Brent range was the futures price; the physical barrel, the one consumer prices follow, traded about $27 higher.

                                                            Scenario replays

                                                            Five episodes, two ways to hedge

                                                            The book alone, with 30% in the 10-year Treasury, and with the manual's hedge stack: a monthly 95/85 put spread on the whole book plus 4% gold and 4% Brent. No hedge wins every episode: the stack wins oil and liquidity shocks, bonds win deflationary busts, and neither saved a slow inflation bear like 2022, where trend-following is the missing leg.

                                                            Reverse DCF: what growth the price assumes
                                                            Implied 10-year growth

                                                            The bridge and the reverse DCFCash EPS = [NI − (Deconomic − Dbook) − SBC − Δcapitalized software + Δdeferred revenue] ÷ diluted shares (pre-tax adjustments: a conservative floor). Reverse DCF: solve g in ∑t=1..10 F0(1+g)t/(1+r)t + F10(1+gT)/((r−gT)(1+r)10) = market value, gT = 3%. Moonshot flag: g > 2 × the last three years' cash growth.

                                                            The six tests, run on every builder

                                                            Healthy, watch or red against the manual's thresholds: capex over depreciation above 2.5x, free cash flow below 60% of net income, stock pay above 12% of revenue, receivables outgrowing revenue by 10 points. Stock pay and receivables fill in from the daily SEC run.

                                                            An unlevered direct-lending fund: base rate 3.9% plus a 5.5% unitranche spread, 1.25% management fee and 12.5% incentive fee. At today's default rate, the illiquidity premium over Treasuries is gone.

                                                            Position tiers and the moonbag rule

                                                            About 4% of US stocks produced all the net wealth creation from 1926 to 2016 (Bessembinder, 2018). Selling winners early is the most expensive error in that distribution, so the framework protects through size and hedges, not early exits.

                                                            Physics · Watts, wafers and concrete

                                                            The AI buildout is limited by watts, not dollars.

                                                            Turn the capex into physical units and the binding constraint shows: the grid, the turbines and the time it takes to build anything large. These sources are not financial: grid auctions, engineering order books, megaproject statistics and economic history.

                                                            Calculator

                                                            From dollars to watts

                                                            What a year of AI capex asks of the grid, at today's cost per gigawatt.

                                                            Cost per gigawatt: about $41B (Brookings, 2025) to about $50B (Nvidia, 2025). Some capex (warehouses, offices) is not AI; treat the result as an upper bound.

                                                            The conversionGW = capex ÷ cost per GW. TWh a year = GW × 8,760 hours × load ÷ 1,000. Homes = TWh × 109 ÷ 10,791 kWh (EIA's 2022 average US home). Share of US use = TWh ÷ 4,000 (176 TWh was 4.4% in 2023).

                                                            The grid

                                                            Demand arrives faster than supply can be built

                                                            History

                                                            The largest build as a share of the economy since the railroads

                                                            Average yearly investment as a share of GDP during each boom (Brookings Papers, 2026). Carlota Perez's work on five technological revolutions finds the same arc each time: installation, a financial frenzy, a turning point (the crash), then a long deployment that pays off for users more than for builders.

                                                                Field · Research outside the screen

                                                                An anecdote is a question. Date it, source it, name what else could explain it, then check the evidence that separates the stories.

                                                                From the fifth review: observations from suppliers, lenders, landlords and job sites often move before the reported numbers. They earn a place in the book only after they are written down with provenance, matched to a later measurable outcome and tested. Nothing on this desk is validated yet; it is the method for getting there.

                                                                Three clocks

                                                                Every observation sits on three clocks, and they rarely agree

                                                                Economic clockWhen the activity actually changed: a supplier asked for deposits, a lender tightened, a lease was signed.
                                                                Publication clockWhen an official series or filing shows it: often a month to two quarters later, then revised.
                                                                Market clockWhen prices reflect it: sometimes before the economic clock (expectations), sometimes long after the publication clock.

                                                                Edge comes from the gaps between the clocks, never from the observation alone. Each note below records the first two dates (event and learned) so the gap can be measured later.

                                                                Compare explanations

                                                                Which story fits, and what to check next

                                                                Pick an observation. Mark what you have checked. Bayes' rule updates the explanations; the ranking shows which unchecked evidence would remove the most doubt (expected information, in bits). The likelihoods are judged, so argue with them.

                                                                    Lab · The math behind the desk

                                                                    Seven toys that explain why the desk does what it does.

                                                                    Each one is a formula the engine uses, made into something you can move. Start with the coin game: it explains leverage, Kelly and Taleb's ruin in one picture.

                                                                    System

                                                                    The engine behind the desk.

                                                                    Python, about 6,500 lines including tests, run every weekday on GitHub Actions. One timing rule runs through all of it: a value at date t uses data through the close of t, and a decision made at t earns returns from t+1.

                                                                    The five stages of the daily run

                                                                    1. Data

                                                                      91 sources: FRED curve, credit, volatility, oil, inflation, jobs, sentiment and financial conditions daily; feeds from Substack, Telegram, X, Reddit and the wires; SEC 10-K and 10-Q facts; 155 years of public data monthly; Databento bars with split and dividend factors; Kalshi odds.

                                                                    2. Exposures

                                                                      Daily betas to market, AI and rates factors. SPCX leans on TSLA's betas until it has its own history.

                                                                    3. Regime

                                                                      Stock-bond correlation, exponentially weighted with a 63-day half-life, read with hysteresis: hedging, neutral or amplifying.

                                                                    4. Hedge & size

                                                                      Min-variance TLT ratio when the regime allows it. Vol target and drawdown cap set gross; Kelly checks the edge.

                                                                    5. Prove

                                                                      Dollar-exact backtest with costs and financing, deflated Sharpe, and walk-forward forecasts judged on calibration.

                                                                    v0.7 · the policy contract

                                                                    Policies, conventions and what each number means

                                                                    Every displayed decision names the policy that made it, and the engine backtests the same function. These are the specifications and the accounting conventions every performance number follows.

                                                                    hedge.tlt.v2

                                                                    Hold TLT at the minimum-variance ratio (capped at 1.0x) only while the stock-bond state is "hedging" and, when the research has a validated inflation line, 36-month inflation is below it. The state enters at a correlation of −0.10 or below and leaves only above 0. A missing input makes the decision unavailable.

                                                                    size.equity.v2

                                                                    Equity scale = the smallest of the volatility target over forecast volatility, the one-year 25% drawdown cap (95% confidence, simulated) and 1.5x. Quarter Kelly is reported beside it as an edge check, never as a size input.

                                                                    limits.portfolio.v1

                                                                    After the hedge is added, equity plus bond notional may not exceed 2.0x NAV; option premium is capped at 2% of NAV. Equity and hedge scale down together when the cap binds.

                                                                    Accounting

                                                                    One NAV series: costs and financing come out of NAV the day they occur, the first trade's cost is in the first return, and the product of returns equals final NAV. Signals at the close of day t trade at the close of t+1. Sharpe is in excess of the cash actually accrued.

                                                                    Comparisons

                                                                    Every variant runs on the same dates after the warm-up, from the same starting NAV, beside an unhedged book and a cash-only baseline. The deflated Sharpe counts every variant, hedge policy and candidate hedge tried.

                                                                    Concentration

                                                                    Effective risk contributors (1 ÷ Σ risk share²) measures concentration by position. Effective independent bets (Meucci, across principal components) measures how many drivers the risk loads on. Two equal, perfectly correlated positions score 2 and 1.
